H1.text: A tailor measures cloth. A builder measures a floor. A painter, a wall.

H2.text: All three combine lengths. And every length hides a small error.

H3.text: Aarav measures his study table. One hundred and twenty centimetres, by sixty.

H4.text: His ruler can be off by one millimetre on each side.

H5.text: So how far off is the area? One square millimetre? It is much bigger.

P2.text: When we calculate with measured values, their errors travel into the result.

P4.text: We always take the worst case, so the true value surely lies inside our range.

S1.text: First, adding. Two rods on our measuring bench.

S2.text: Rod A is twenty centimetres, plus or minus zero point one.

S3.text: Rod B is fifteen, plus or minus zero point one.

S4.text: End to end, the total is thirty five centimetres.

S5.text: Let both rods be at their longest. The total grows by zero point two.

S6.text: Both at their shortest, it shrinks by zero point two.

S7.text: So it is thirty five, plus or minus zero point two. The errors added up.

B1.text: Now subtract. Lay rod B along rod A. Five centimetres stick out.

B3.text: Longest case: A at its longest, B at its shortest. Five point two.

B4.text: Shortest case: the other way round. Four point eight.

B5.text: So it is five, plus or minus zero point two. Even when we subtract, the errors add.

D1.text: Let's write this as a rule, one step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. Z equals A plus B, with errors delta A and delta B.

D3.text: Step two. The biggest Z is A plus delta A, plus B plus delta B.

D4.text: Step three. So the error in Z is delta A plus delta B. The same holds for A minus B.

T1.text: Remember this. When you add or subtract, the absolute errors add.

K1.text: Side by side. Adding gave thirty five, plus or minus zero point two.

K2.text: Subtracting gave five. The same error, on a much smaller answer.

K3.text: Now you try. Fifty plus or minus one, minus thirty plus or minus one. Is the error zero, or two? Pause and decide.

K4.text: Two! Errors never cancel. One reading can be high while the other is low.

M1.text: Now multiply. Back to Aarav's table.

M2.text: One twenty by sixty is seven thousand two hundred square centimetres.

M3.text: Now stretch both sides by one millimetre. Two thin strips appear.

M5.text: The long strip is one hundred and twenty times zero point one. Twelve square centimetres.

M6.text: The short strip is sixty times zero point one. Six. The tiny corner is too small to count.

M8.text: So the area can be off by eighteen square centimetres, not one square millimetre!

M9.text: Make the table narrower, and the percentage error climbs. A short side brings more error.

R1.text: Now the rule for multiplying, step by step.

R2.text: Step one. Z equals A times B. The extra area is A delta B, plus B delta A.

R3.text: Step two. Divide both sides by Z, which is A times B.

R4.text: Step three. Delta Z over Z equals delta A over A, plus delta B over B. The relative errors add.

R5.text: Step four. For Z equals A over B, the rule is the same.

C1.text: Side by side. Adding or subtracting: add the absolute errors, in centimetres.

C2.text: Multiplying or dividing: add the relative errors, which have no unit. Or the percentages.

C3.text: Your turn. Speed is distance over time. Distance has one percent error, time has two. Is the speed error one percent, or three? Pause.

C4.text: Three percent! Division still adds the relative errors. They never subtract.

W1.text: Now, one worked example. Aarav's table, done fully.

W2.text: Length one twenty, width sixty, each plus or minus zero point one centimetres.

W3.text: Relative error in length: zero point one over one hundred and twenty.

W4.text: Relative error in width: zero point one over sixty.

W5.text: Add them. Zero point zero zero two five, or zero point two five percent.

W6.text: Seven thousand two hundred times zero point zero zero two five gives eighteen.

W7.text: So the area is seven thousand two hundred, plus or minus eighteen square centimetres.

X2.text: Many students subtract the errors when they subtract values.

X3.text: But errors always add. Delta Z is still delta A plus delta B.

E1.text: Where is this asked? As numericals on the maximum percentage error in a result.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Find the maximum percentage error in the trolley's average speed. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is C. One point four percent.

A2.text: The distance is fifty centimetres. Its error is zero point one plus zero point one, zero point two.

A3.text: That is zero point four percent. The time error is zero point zero two over two, one percent.

A4.text: Speed is a division, so add them. One point four percent.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Why do errors add, even when you subtract?

Y3.text: Two. When do you add percentage errors instead?

Y4.text: Three. What is the error in the perimeter of Aarav's table?

N1.text: Next time: your calculator shows eight digits. Which ones do you keep? Measurement uncertainty.
